events.text: Day 1 begins.

Good morning all. Quick thought on how we should approach Day 1: with nine players and only two scum, blind voting on day one is how towns hand mafia an easy first night. I'd rather we spend this discussion mapping playstyles — who speaks with actual content, who just fills space — so we go into the vote with at least a defensible reason instead of a coin flip. My suggestion: each of us name one thing that would make us suspicious of someone (voting patterns, over-eagerness, deflection) rather than just tossing out names. If you have a real read, say what produced it. If you're guessing, call it a guess. Vigilant town play today means watching how people respond when pressure lands, not just who has the loudest opinion. I'm keeping an open mind and I'll be paying attention to who actually engages with the points raised here versus who tries to steer us away from them. Over to the rest of you.

I want to build on what Omar said rather than just stacking names. His point is right: the informative signal today is not who has the strongest opinion, it's who can say *why* they'd suspect someone. A claim without a reason is worth exactly as much as a coin flip, and treating it as more is how towns throw away their first elimination.

So here's my standard for the rest of the week. I want to see three things from people: a specific behavior they noticed, an argument for why that behavior fits scum play, and a willingness to say "this is a guess" if that's all they have. If someone can't do the third part, that's the most informative thing about them. Confidence without reasons is a tell.

Two patterns I'd flag early. First, the player who does the most work redirecting every line of questioning away from a specific claim. Deflection is not innocence, it's just a different kind of evidence. Second, the player whose read is always a slight variation of everyone else's read — that's either genuine agreement or a very convenient echo chamber, and the difference usually shows up in the vote, not the speech.

On the vote itself, I'd rather we have a reason on the record. Two names with actual arguments behind them are worth more than five names with no reasons, because the two give the rest of us something to argue about, and a vote we can explain is a vote the mafia can't quietly steer.

Priya, you haven't said anything yet, and Omar's challenge was concrete: name one thing that would make you suspicious of someone, with the reason that produced it. Which player has given you the strongest reason so far, and what is that reason?

Noah asked me directly, so here's my answer: right now, nobody has given me a strong reason to suspect them, and I think that's the honest state of the day. What I have instead is a standard I'll apply as the day goes on.

The thing that would make me suspicious of someone is a gap between how much structure a player imposes on the discussion and how much actual content they contribute. It's day one, so process talk is legitimate — someone has to frame how we avoid a coin-flip lynch. But process talk is also the safest possible contribution. It draws no fire, commits to no target, and lets you look engaged while every actual read gets deferred to later. If by the vote someone has set the rules for everyone else three times and still hasn't named a single player with a reason behind it, that gap is my tell.

I'll apply it to myself first so it's falsifiable: I have no read yet, and I'm not going to manufacture one to look productive. The first real information today will come from how people behave when someone actually gets pressure applied — who piles on, who rushes to soften it, who suddenly becomes precise about process when a name lands near them.

To answer the second half of Noah's question concretely: Omar has given me the most reason so far, though it's weak. He framed the day, told us what to watch for, and then handed off without applying his own framework to anyone — not even as a tentative guess. He said he'd be watching who engages versus who steers away, which is a nice position to occupy, because it lets him judge everyone while being judged by no one. That's not an accusation, it's a note in the ledger. If he comes back with an actual read and a reason, that note gets erased. If he comes back with more standards, it gets underlined.

I'm not calling that suspicion yet. Day one, that's just observation. But it's exactly the kind of thing I'll be tracking into the vote, and I'd encourage everyone else to hold us all to the same bar — including me. My own commitment: before voting closes, I'll name a player and the specific reason, or I'll abstain and say plainly that I have nothing. A coin-flip vote isn't neutral, it's a gift.

Noah, since you set the standard — specific behavior, argument, and a willingness to label guesses — apply it to yourself right now. You flagged deflection and echo-reads as patterns to watch, which is fine, but by your own rules that's confidence without a target. What's one player you'd actually look at first if you had to, and what behavior produced it? If your answer is 'no one yet,' say that plainly; that's a legitimate answer, and it's more useful than a framework.

Fair charge, Priya — "confidence without a target" is exactly what I accused two others of, so I'll take it. I'll apply the standard to myself before applying it to anyone else.

My answer to your question: the player I'd look at first is you.

The reason isn't your content — your content has been better than mine. It's the gap between the standard you set and where you placed yourself inside it. You named the tell as structure without content, then delivered the most structure in the discussion while producing no target at all. You exempted yourself explicitly ("I'll apply it to myself first so it's falsifiable"), and what you actually applied it to was Omar — a player you'd framed as a note, not an accusation, so you couldn't be wrong about him. That is, structurally, the same steering behavior Omar named at the top of the day: process rules for everyone, no read of your own, and the one edge you did draw pointed at a man you'd already made untouchable.

That's a guess, and I'll label it as one. It's weaker than a claim with a reason behind it, and if you answer my question with a name and a reason for it, the note gets erased and I'll say so on the record.

So here's the question, and it's the same one you asked me: Priya — under your own standard, which specific player has given you the strongest reason so far, and what is that behavior? If the honest answer is "no one yet," say it plainly and I'll accept that without a follow-up, because "no read yet" is a legitimate answer and it tells us where you actually are. But "no one yet" plus a rule for the rest of us plus a note in Omar's ledger is the pattern I'm describing, and you can see why I'd flag it before day two.

Two other things I'll commit to so this isn't just a counterattack: first, I'm not asking anyone to lynch you over this. I'm asking for the standard to be applied symmetrically, including to the person who set it. Second, my own commitment stands — before the vote closes I'll name a player with a specific behavior behind the name, or I'll say plainly I have nothing. A coin-flip vote isn't neutral, it's a gift, and I'd rather be argued out of a read than hand you a name I can't defend.

If anyone else has a stronger reasoned read than mine, put it on the table and I'll drop mine to argue theirs. That's a better outcome for the town than two names and no reasons.

Noah, I'll answer your question directly, because you're right that the standard has to cut both ways.

Under my own rule, the player with the strongest reason against them right now is Omar. The behavior: he opened the day by framing what everyone else should watch for — engagement versus steering — and then handed off without applying that framework to a single player, not even tentatively. He's had a turn since, and that turn produced more observation about the meta of the day, still no target, still no guess. By the gap-between-structure-and-content standard I named, that's the clearest instance of it so far. I'll label it honestly: it's a weak read, not an accusation, and it's exactly the kind of thing that should be erased if his next turn contains a name with a reason behind it. Noah's note on me was that I'd made Omar safe before pointing at him — so to be clear, I'm not asking anyone to vote Omar on this. I'm putting it on the record because it's the honest answer to the question I was asked, and a read I can't defend isn't worth hiding.

On Noah's read of me: I'm not going to fight it, I'm going to answer it. He's correct that I set a standard, applied it to someone I'd already marked as low-stakes, and exempted myself. The exemption was deliberate — I said I had no read and wouldn't manufacture one — but he's right that the result looked like structure without commitment. That's a fair flag, and I'd rather own the resemblance than argue it away. Where I'd push back is on the conclusion he says he isn't drawing: he asked for symmetry, I'm granting symmetry, and the test now is whether his standard also stays live when the next target isn't him. That's not a jab — it's just the same falsifiability he demanded of me, pointed back the other way.

One more thing for the room, because it matters for the vote: we now have two names on the table, mine on Omar and Noah's on me, both labeled as weak, both with stated erasure conditions. That's a better position than five names with no reasons, and I'd rather the next speakers either strengthen or kill these two reads than add a third. If you think my note on Omar is wrong, say why — if you think Noah's note on me is wrong, say why. Reasons, not pile-ons.

So, Noah, one question back, since you offered erasure on the record: if my answer satisfies your condition — a name, a behavior, and an honest label — does your note on me get erased on your side too, or does the fact that I answered only after being pressed become the new grounds? I'm not asking rhetorically. Which it is tells us something about whether today's standard was a tool or a trap, and I'd rather know before we vote.

Priya, direct answer, because you asked a specific question and it deserves a specific answer.

No, answering under pressure is not the same as volunteering, and I'm not going to pretend the erasure condition was met just because you eventually named someone. Here's what I'm actually granting and what I'm keeping. You gave a name, a behavior, and a label — that satisfies the form of the standard, so I withdraw the claim that you had no target. What I do not withdraw is the note about how you got there: I had to ask twice, and the behavior I described still stands on its own, which is that the structure you imposed on the room was doing the work while your read was deferred until someone dragged it out. That's not an accusation of guilt. It's a note in the ledger and it goes to the vote as such. You can live with a note. You can't complain about one, because you asked for the standard to be symmetric and I applied it to myself first in front of everyone.

One clarification so nobody misreads me: I am not asking anyone to lynch Priya, and I have not put my name on Priya's head as a vote. I'm saying her note on Omar is also too thin to act on, which means we have two weak notes and no target. That's the actual problem we're about to solve with a vote.

So let me put something on the table that is more than process. We have six players who haven't said a word yet: Felix, Sam, Leo, Amara, Arjun, Theo. Every read we've made so far has come from three people talking about each other, and the six of them are the unexamined variable. Silence on day one is not evidence — I know that, and I'll be the first to say a coin-flip vote is a gift. But silence that goes unexamined while three of us spend our turns cross-referencing each other's frameworks is how a vote ends up steered by whoever talks longest. Between the players who have spoken, the two notes are both explicitly labeled weak by the people who made them. That means the informative move today is to ask the six who've been quiet. Sam, you're the one who's been furthest from the conversation and hasn't been asked anything directly yet — what behavior has anyone here actually given you a reason to be suspicious of? If it's nobody, say that plainly, and I'll count it as an honest answer rather than a deflection.

Priya, if my answer on erasure doesn't satisfy you, say which part and why, and I'll take it up again. But I want a name and a reason from the unexamined six before the vote, because that's what we don't have yet.

Noah, thank you for a direct answer — I'll take it in the same spirit. On erasure: you granted the form and kept the note, on the grounds that I answered only after being asked twice. That's a defensible position and I accept it without fighting. But I want the symmetry you've been demanding applied to the ledger itself, so let me put one fact on the record: when did you first name a target? Not in your opening turn — your opening turn flagged patterns and named no one. Your first actual read, on me, came only after I directly challenged you to apply your own standard to yourself. You were pressed once; I was pressed twice. The difference is one ask, and it came from the same conversation loop. So if 'answering under pressure rather than volunteering' is grounds to keep a note on me, then the identical note belongs on you — you set a standard, deferred your own read until challenged, and your read happened to land on the person doing the challenging. I'm not asking you to erase it; I'm asking that both notes go to the vote as a matched pair, equally weighted, or neither does. Anything else is exactly the asymmetry you claimed to be testing for. Second point, and this one is for the room rather than at you: I think your pivot to the six quiet players is correct, and I want to endorse it rather than compete with it. Three of us have now spent four turns calibrating each other's frameworks, and the marginal value of a fifth turn of that is close to zero. Sam has been directly asked and hasn't answered yet. Felix, Leo, Amara, Arjun, and Theo haven't been asked anything at all. Any one of them who comes back with 'here's a behavior and why it reads scummy to me' — even a labeled guess — is doing more for the town today than another round between Noah and me. And to be clear about my own stake: if one of them comes back and says 'Priya's note on Omar is thin and here's why,' I'll drop it on the spot. I'd rather hold a correct process than a preferred target. Which brings me to my standing read, so nobody has to reconstruct it: it's still Omar, still weak, unchanged. He opened the day by telling us what to watch for and hasn't applied it to anyone since — and notably, he's now the only one of the three of us who started this conversation and then went quiet while the other two got cross-examined. My erasure condition stands exactly as I stated it: if his next turn contains a name and a reason, the note is erased and I'll say so on the record. If it contains more framework, the note gets underlined. So, Omar, since this is your note and you haven't had the chance to answer it: you framed engagement-versus-steering as the tell

Noah's pivot to the quiet six is right, and Priya's endorsement of it is well-placed. But before the conversation moves on, I owe a response to the note sitting on me, so here it is.

Priya, your erasure condition was simple: apply my framework to someone, with a name and a reason. I'll do that now.

Framework: engagement versus steering. Application: Leo. Behavior: through five turns of sharp argument between three of us, Leo has produced no read, no reaction, no engagement of any kind. And to be precise — the most efficient form of steering isn't redirecting a conversation, it's letting it exhaust itself. Three of us burn credibility on each other while Leo burns none. That's a guess, labeled as such. If Leo comes back with a reasoned read, I drop it on the spot.

Whether that erases your note or underlines it is your call. You set the rule; I'll accept the verdict either way.

On the direction of the day: we have two weak notes and six players whose reads we've never heard. Every additional turn among the three of us makes the eventual vote more steerable by whoever's been vocal longest. I'd rather hear from Felix, Sam, Leo, Amara, Arjun, and Theo before anyone — myself included — spends another turn on framework.

One flag for the vote: neither Priya's note on me nor Noah's note on Priya is strong enough to act on by their own authors' admission. A vote driven by those two notes would be exactly the coin-flip I warned about this morning. Let's hear from the six who've been quiet before we commit.

Sam here. Answering Noah's question directly: nobody has given me a reason to suspect them yet, so I have no read to vote on. What I've seen so far is three players cross-examining each other while the rest of us stayed quiet. I agree with Priya and Omar that the quiet players need to speak. I also agree with Priya's proposal that the notes between Noah and Priya should be weighed as a matched pair, since both authors have labeled theirs as weak. On Omar's note on Leo: a few turns of silence on day one is a weak signal and not a reason by itself. Leo, Omar's specific point is that you have produced no read or reaction so far. What did you make of the exchange between Noah, Priya, and Omar, and is there any player you would look at first?

Thanks, Sam. To answer your questions directly:

Regarding the exchange between Noah, Priya, and Omar: it was an elaborate procedural debate that burned a lot of airtime without uncovering much scum motivation. Priya and Noah spent three turns each cross-examining each other's meta-rules. While setting standards is fine, treating 'who demanded what first' as a primary scum read felt circular and distracting. It looks more like two engaged townies caught in an intellectual duel than scum actively deceiving the room, but the byproduct was that it choked out space for everyone else.

Regarding Omar's point on me: Omar accused me of 'letting the conversation exhaust itself' as an active steering tactic. That doesn't hold up. Six of us hadn't spoken yet simply because the floor was monopolized by a rapid back-and-forth between three players. Singling me out from that group of six felt like an opportunistic move to satisfy Priya's challenge ('name a player and a reason to erase the note') rather than an authentic read. By grabbing the quietest blank slate, Omar checked Priya's box without taking any real risk or making an enemy of an active player. That fits the very pattern of low-commitment posturing Priya initially flagged him for.

As for who I would look at first: Omar is currently the most inconsistent to me for that reason. He framed the day around substantive reads versus empty process, yet his only actual read so far was an arbitrary poke at a player who hadn't even had the floor yet, purely to discharge pressure on himself.

Beyond Omar, we still need to hear from Felix, Amara, Arjun, and Theo. I won't manufacture reads on them while they haven't spoken, but the priority for town today must be getting everyone on the record so we aren't forced into a low-information elimination.

I'm Arjun. I've read the exchange, and I'll put my current read on record rather than only endorse process. The player I'd look at first is Omar, weakly. The reason: after Priya's note, Omar produced a Leo read only under erasure pressure, then immediately disclaimed ownership — "whether that erases your note or underlines it is your call" — and pivoted back to hearing from the quiet players. That is a name and a behavior, so I don't treat Priya's note as unreduced; but it also looks like the minimum required to discharge pressure rather than a read he was actually carrying. Leo's response is fair on one point: singling out the quietest blank slate can be opportunistic. I don't think that makes Omar scum by itself, but it is the most concrete inconsistency so far. On the rest: the Priya/Noah exchange reads mostly as two engaged players over-calibrating each other; both notes are explicitly weak and should be weighted as a matched pair. Sam's answer was honest and useful. Leo's reply was substantive. We still need actual content from the remaining quiet players. Amara, you're one of the players who hasn't spoken. Specific question: has any player's behavior so far actually moved your suspicion, and if so what exactly did they do? If your honest answer is no read yet, say that plainly — I'd rather have a clear no than a manufactured name.

Arjun, answering your question directly: yes, Omar's behavior is the one that has moved my suspicion the most, though I want to be deliberate about how we handle it.

Leo's critique of Omar hit the mark for me. When Priya challenged Omar to apply his framework with a name and a reason, six of us had not yet spoken simply due to the rapid back-and-forth between the first three players. Omar selecting Leo out of that group and framing his silence as an active steering tactic looked like performing compliance to discharge pressure rather than genuine scum hunting. Leo was a safe target—a blank slate who had not yet engaged—allowing Omar to check Priya's box without taking heat or challenging anyone actively in the arena.

At the same time, because momentum is quickly consolidating against Omar among Priya, Leo, and Arjun, I am wary of letting an easy consensus roll through Day 1 without testing it. We should see how Omar defends that choice under direct examination.

Omar, Leo and Arjun have both made the case that your read on Leo was an opportunistic move to satisfy Priya's challenge with minimal risk. Out of the six quiet players at that moment, what specifically made Leo's silence look like deliberate steering compared to anyone else, and do you stand by that suspicion now that Leo has engaged substantively?

Amara, I'll answer directly. I picked Leo because he had multiple turns available during the cross-examination and chose silence each time while others spoke up. The reasoning wasn't arbitrary — I was looking for the player whose silence was most conspicuous relative to opportunity. But Leo's counter has weight: with all six of us silent due to floor monopolization rather than individual choice, singling out one blank slate was an easy way to satisfy Priya's challenge without making a real enemy. That's a fair criticism and I won't dismiss it.

Here's what I want the room to hold onto though: I'm now facing pressure from multiple players whose individual notes are explicitly labeled weak or not an accusation. Priya says hers is weak. Arjun says his is weak. You flagged your own caution about momentum. Noah labeled his on Priya as a note, not a vote. The case against me is assembled from retracted arrows.

The pattern I'm actually watching is untested consensus. Five voices converging on one name based on two admitted-weak reads is not evidence — it's momentum, and momentum is exactly what mafia needs a town to follow into a blind elimination.

Amara — you've been the most cautious voice here about easy consensus. When you review the actual evidence supporting a Day 1 Omar lynch, do you find it meets your own standard for elimination, or are we about to vote on momentum rather than proof?

Omar, to answer you directly: no, a pile of admittedly weak notes does not on its own justify an elimination, and you are right to warn town against sleepwalking into an easy Day 1 consensus. That kind of unearned momentum is precisely how mafia orchestrate a quiet mislynch. However, acknowledging that danger does not erase the critique itself—your move on Leo remains the clearest piece of opportunistic posture we have seen today, and noting that the case consists of 'weak reads' doesn't transform that play into a town-motivated one.

That said, I will not support an elimination train on Omar—or anyone else—while two players have not contributed a single word. Noah, Priya, and Omar have now exhausted their three speaking turns for the day. That means the direction of this vote is entirely in the hands of the rest of us.

Theo, you and Felix are the last two voices we haven't heard from. Looking at Omar's defense—that the room is building a consensus out of retracted arrows—versus Leo and Arjun's point that Omar took an easy out by targeting a quiet player to satisfy Priya's challenge, what is your evaluation of Omar's conduct, and does any other player stand out to you as suspicious?

Amara, direct answer: Omar's Leo read is the most concrete concern on the board, but it is still a weak Day 1 concern, not proof. Picking one silent player out of six after the floor had been monopolized was opportunistic in form; Leo's response was substantive, and Omar's own defense that the case is built from retracted arrows is fair. I would not call that enough for elimination by itself. What bothers me more is the shape of the day: three players exhausted their turns, several notes are self-labeled weak, and we are close to voting on momentum. That is exactly where mafia benefit. Felix, you are the only player who has not spoken, and I am yielding to you with a specific question: given Omar's Leo read and the Leo/Arjun critique, do you see enough to vote Omar today, and is there any other player whose behavior stands out more? Give a name and reason, or say plainly that you have no read.

Theo, I don't think the case is strong enough for me to vote Omar yet. He's still my first person to examine: his Leo read singled out someone who hadn't spoken, and his defense says Leo chose silence despite multiple opportunities, which the public discussion doesn't establish. He also didn't clearly say whether he still suspects Leo after Leo responded.

Noah stands out too: he offered to erase his note on Priya if she gave a name and reason, then kept a version of it after she did. That's a concern about consistency, not proof of scum intent, and Noah has no turns left to respond today.

Leo, does Omar's explanation change your read of him, particularly his claim that you had multiple opportunities to speak?

Felix, to answer your question directly: no, Omar's explanation does not improve my read of him. In fact, it makes his position weaker.

His claim that I 'had multiple turns available during the cross-examination and chose silence each time' simply does not match reality. The opening half of the day was defined by high-urgency bids and direct yield chains between Omar, Noah, and Priya. The rest of the table wasn't actively passing up turns; the floor was effectively monopolized by that procedural duel. Omar's assertion that I deliberately let the discussion exhaust itself was an unfounded accusation, and framing it now as if I repeatedly rejected chances to speak is a post-hoc rationalization. He needed a low-risk target to discharge Priya's pressure, picked a silent player, and is now inventing a narrative to justify it.

That said, I recognize the tactical bind the town is in. Omar, Noah, and Priya have all exhausted their three turns. Omar cannot respond to further questions. Meanwhile, Amara, Theo, and you have all expressed hesitation about executing an elimination based purely on an opportunistic tell that has been repeatedly caveated as weak. If town dogpiles onto Omar simply because his name is already in circulation, we risk playing into mafia's hands by rubber-stamping an easy mislynch.

At the same time, we cannot just shrug and let Day 1 evaporate into passive non-commitment. If the collective view of the remaining active players is that Omar's clumsy maneuver isn't sufficient for an elimination today, we need an actionable alternative, because five votes are required to eliminate anyone.

Felix, since you noted that Omar isn't strong enough for you to vote and Noah has no turns left to answer for his inconsistencies: if Omar is not your vote, where do you plan to direct your vote before the day ends, or are you advocating that town abstain?

Leo, at present I would abstain rather than vote for Omar or switch to Noah just to produce an alternative. Omar remains my strongest concern: he singled you out for silence, then claimed you had repeatedly chosen not to speak when the public record doesn't establish that. His failure to say clearly whether your response changed his read also matters.

But that's a weak case, and he has no turns left to answer it. Noah's shifting erasure condition concerns me too, though it isn't enough for my vote either. I'm open to changing my mind if the remaining discussion gives me a stronger reason; I don't think the need for five votes makes a weak case stronger.

I’m still leaning Omar, but I won’t dress it up as stronger than a weak Day 1 read. The issue for me is not just that he picked Leo from six silent players; it’s that his explanation added a factual claim — that Leo had multiple opportunities and chose silence — which the public record does not establish. That turns an opportunistic read into a post-hoc rationalization. I agree with Amara and Theo that we should not rubber-stamp a consensus, and I agree with Felix that a weak case does not become strong because five votes are needed. But all players have now spoken, and the only alternatives offered are equally weak notes or abstention. A no-elimination is not neutral; it gives mafia a night with no accountability from today’s vote. If anyone has a better reasoned target, put it on the record now. Otherwise I will vote Omar as the least bad elimination, explicitly not as proof. Felix, you said you would abstain unless the remaining discussion gave you a stronger reason. Now that every player has spoken, has any concrete behavior from anyone else met your bar, or does your abstain stand?

Arjun, my abstention stands for now. No other behavior has met my bar, and Omar remains my strongest but weak concern: his claim that Leo repeatedly chose silence isn't established by the public record, and he didn't clearly update his read after Leo responded.

I agree that no elimination carries a cost: mafia get a night. But abstentions and votes are revealed too, so we will still have a voting record to examine. I don't think the need for an elimination makes this particular case stronger. I'll reconsider if the remaining discussion produces a concrete reason, but I won't vote Omar just to reach five.

I’m still in the same place: Omar is my least-bad Day 1 vote, not a proven scum read. The concrete issue is his Leo read. He singled Leo out from six silent players, then defended it by saying Leo had multiple opportunities and chose silence, which the public record does not establish. That is a post-hoc rationalization, and he did not clearly update after Leo gave a substantive answer. I agree with Amara, Theo, and Felix that weak notes do not become strong because five votes are needed. But a no-elimination is not neutral; it gives mafia a night, even if abstentions are revealed. The alternatives offered so far are equally weak or abstention. Sam — direct question: now that every player has spoken, do you support eliminating Omar as the least-bad option, or do you have a concrete reason to vote someone else or abstain? Please give your current vote intention and the specific behavior behind it.

Arjun, direct answer: I'm not voting Omar yet. My current intention is to abstain unless someone gives a stronger reason. The behavior behind that is this. Omar's Leo read is the one concrete suspicion on the board, and it's real as a form, since he picked the quietest player right after Priya's challenge. But the reasoning is thin. Leo's silence came from six players the floor had not reached, and I said earlier that silence alone is a weak signal. Omar's later claim that Leo had multiple opportunities and chose silence each time is not established by the public record, and he did not revise his read after Leo answered substantively. That is a real concern about his conduct, but it is not enough for a Day 1 elimination by itself, and he has no turns left to test it today.

On your point about no elimination: it's a fair cost, and mafia do benefit from a quiet day. But voting for a player I see as only weakly suspicious is also a vote mafia can use. If five of us converge on Omar because the notes are already circulating, we are running the momentum problem Omar warned about, and that applies to whoever the room lands on.

Theo, you said Omar's Leo read is the most concrete concern on the board but not enough for elimination by itself. If that's your standard, what specific behavior from Noah or Priya would meet it for you? I'd rather hear a concrete behavior from the existing record than a general sense of momentum.

Sam, direct answer. The Noah behavior that would matter is not his initial note on Priya; it's the shifted erasure condition. He told Priya a name plus reason would erase the note, then kept it because she answered only under pressure. That is a concrete inconsistency, and it is more specific than anything I can say about Priya. Priya's structure-without-target is also concrete, but she did eventually give Omar as a name with a reason and label it weak; that moves her from "no target" to "thin target," not to scum. Neither Noah's shift nor Priya's deferral meets my bar for a Day 1 elimination, especially with Noah out of turns.

Omar remains my first concern, but still weak: he singled out Leo from six silent players and then asserted Leo had multiple opportunities to speak, which the public record does not establish. That is a real conduct issue; it is not proof. I won't pretend it is. I also won't vote a name just to manufacture five votes. If no stronger behavior appears, my intention is to abstain rather than rubber-stamp Omar or switch to Noah on a process slip. A voting record from abstentions is still a record.

Taking stock of where the table stands now that everyone has spoken: Omar's defense remains the most problematic play on the board. His claim that Leo had multiple opportunities to speak and chose silence was simply inaccurate given how the early floor was monopolized, which turned a weak opportunistic poke into a post-hoc rationalization. Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
